story_text.value:
Hi HN. Euspell is a conservastive respelling of English and all the software needed to implement it. The link above converts the text you paste, in your browser. Other ways to try it out are the browser extensions and EPUB/PDF readers.

Previous spelling reforms have failed for two reasons: they asked people to apply rules by hand or remember a large set of new spellings, and they couldn't handle homographs: "read" is reed or red, "records" is a noun or a verb, "wound" is an injury or a past tense - writing in pure phonetics will actually create hundreds of homographs. Euspell approaches spelling reform differently, with the goal of aiding reading and comprehension.

- A lexicon with 205505 entries, each with CLAWS7 part-of-speech tags. Of these, 164067 (80%) are left unchanged. No diacritics are used. Proper nouns are untouched. American spelling is the base, in the line of Webster's reforms. - 5920 entries are ambiguous and need context. The noun/verb -s split (records/recordz) is a linear SVM: 93.2% on held-out text. The hand-written rule it replaced scored 75.9%. The full evaluation is at https://github.com/ossiak/euspell/blob/main/docs/paper-evalu... - Semantic splits (e.g. bow, tear, lead) are hand-written rules and less accurate: "read" gets about four in five right on its test set. - Runs locally in a browser extension (Chrome/Firefox/Safari, including PDFs), MS Word, LibreOffice, Google Docs, and a standalone EPUB/PDF reader for Windows, MacOS, Android and iOS. - Code is GPL-3.0, lexicon is CC BY-SA 4.0: https://github.com/ossiak/euspell. White paper: https://euspell.org/paper

The changes can be toggled on and off: Euspell changes what you read, not the source text. AI tools (Claude) helped with the software, the site and the videos; the reform and the lexicon are mine. There is also a 14-part video series: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLfCd5hTV7IWg

Most useful feedback: sentences where it picks the wrong spelling.

story_text.value:
I put this repo and site together as an educational reference for folks getting started with Jev / OpenAI Decisions API.

This demonstrates how Jev can drive a browser (the idea being extract it into a skills file). On every step the page's controls are extracted into a table, and Jev picks an operation and a target, with a probability for every option.

Try the HN login replay (https://jev-browser.rovira.sh/#hackernews-login), Amazon (https://jev-browser.rovira.sh/#amazon-cart), or run it live with your own key.

Interesting bits: - Jev mean response time is 250ms (123–495 ms on the HN run). - Jev never sees the DOM, only a table of controls extracted from it ahead of time. It's in some ways, similar to the accessibility tree that good LLM browser skills use now. - Jev can't generate text (in a good way) so this need to be provided ahead of time, either by you or a complementary LLM. - Each step is stateless and costs a few thousand input tokens, under a tenth of a cent.

Repo (three files, no dependencies): https://github.com/zurfyx/jev-browser-skill

story_text.value:
I am avid reader of blogs (always been since 2005 onwards), so it was always on my list to build a rss reader at some point.

Initially I've built lectura for myself (the first version started when I've experimented with server side rendering/Thymeleaf + Spring Boot) and self hosted on a server (without a domain). Then I decided to vibecode multi user support. And this is the final result.

What are some highlights:

- It doesn't track/record what the users are doing. There are no emails (no password recovering in case you lose your password). The only information that's kept are your own subscription, that others can see as well. But that's it. Because of this, creating a username takes 5 seconds (depending on how fast you write);

- It supports different layouts that I find useful with my RSS reader. For example there's a 'random' content view so you can read "historical articles" you've might missed. There's a another view called 'Quiet Sources' so you can 'prioritise' blogs that don't publish often. I'll let you find the other views.

- It has good accesibility support, or it should. If not, drop me some feedback;

- For the moment it's free. I don't expect a big influx of users (who uses a RSS reader + reading blogs nowadays) so I have a cheap dedicated server at 20$ per month. With the current resources, unless someone really wants to "put it down", it should work with a few hundred users (reading concurrently). I can afford paying 20$ montly withouthing thinking to ask for money, at least for the moment.

That's it.

I don't have experience with 'products', 'startups', etc. This is just a project I hope will be useful to someone other than me. If not, i will keep using it as my "premium" RSS reader :).

Cheers, Andrei

Hi HN, I'm Matt. I just open-sourced my personal agent. If you're interested, paste this into Claude Code or Codex on a Mac:

"Clone github.com/mattabate/life-distributable and set up my life agent. Follow its SETUP.md."

What's cool about the agent:

- It's software distributed as a prompt. No installer, no package, no config.

- The prompt builds a Desktop and iPhone app for communicating with the agent. You can ask the agent to update or refactor the Desktop and iPhone apps to match your desired user experience and use case.

- Mine keeps me on my daily routine, manages my finances and runs a P&L on itself that has stayed positive. When it hit +$200 I bought it Claude Max. When it hit +$1,600, I bought it a Mac mini.

Let me know what you think.

story_text.value:
I have been self-hosting for 10 years, and "family hosting" for 2.

The number of attacks my servers get has increased by 3x since May of this year. Now personally, I don't like hiding behind Cloudflare because I don't want them to be a SPOF, but it was becoming a bit too scary to just be open to the web. Because it is a family cloud, it can't hide behind a VPN, it has to support devices like TV sticks that can't connect properly over VPN. It has to support HTTPS.

So I put together a Rust/Ratatui TUI+cron/CLI that manages my second line of defense: firewall and HTTP server. I run a reverse Nginx proxy in front of apps like Nextcloud, and a nftables firewall with SSH as my admin tunnel. It does several things:

1) It allows me to block entire segments, countries, datacenter IP ranges, TOR exit nodes etc...

2) It allows me to block specific bots: search bots, AI bots, security scanners

3) It does dynamic blocking too, looking at the logs to spot bad behavior and block it. I used to run fail2ban for SSH for example, but a centralized UI for both SSH and HTTP(S) is nicer IMHO.

So if this is useful to anyone else, feel free. It's AGPL v3.

In my experience, geoblocking is the biggest win, reducing the attacks by 30x.

AI Disclosure: I use AI assisted development. I follow Linus Torvalds and Bob Martin model, with using AI as a tool and verifying the result.

story_text.value:
We have built KeibiDrop because me and the people close to me were tired of cloud storages, and to copy data fully across our devices in order to use it.

Now with KeibiDrop you can mount and stream folders between your computers (and web browser) access and edit data on-demand as if it was local.

You can try it instantly in the browser https://web.keibidrop.com/ (you need two devices) or by building from source/ downloading from the github releases. (there are also demo recordings in the Readme on github).

We also got a marketing website for it here: https://keibidrop.com

The desktop app, engine and CLI are FOSS AGPL-v3 and in terms of architecture and stack the following holds:

- It uses a full-duplex P2P IPv6 connection between peers with a fallback to a data forwarding relay.

- We got a dual networking stack QUIC + TCP using protocol buffers (WebRTC to be added), and we use ML-KEM-1024 + X25519 for the handshake and either aes-gcm-256 or chacha20-poly1305 for the session, and we do a latency hiding re-key inspired by Signal's SPQR.

- it relies on FUSE, macFUSE, and WinFsp as filesystem drivers and the whole gist of it is to "hide the latency" of remote filesystems and to just give the feeling of teleporting files.

- we use golang for the engine, and rust + slint.dev for the GUI

Our goal was to have a lightweight, cross platform filesystem that does not use many resources, has the RAM usage bounded and gives the feeling as if working on a local filesystem.

Currently the filesystem respects POSIX semantics, (except for symlinks and hardlinks, I have them disabled), and we tested it on intercontinental links (between Romania and Singapore), on both relayed connections and direct connections.

You can use git, pijul, Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve or any tools you would normally use on your local computer, or use our docker image on your NAS storage and instantly access the data you need while you are travelling.

story_text.value:
I've worked for a long time in the storage field during my career and ZFS is the piece of engineering I admire most in that space. I wanted a way to pay homage to it and to explore and better understand its internals. So I built Uberblok: a museum of ZFS. A deep dive into copy-on-write, txgs, vdevs, RAID-Z, snapshots, the ARC, metaslabs, the ZIL, send/receive with explanations and animated diagrams.

I'm sure people here know these internals better than I do, so corrections are very welcome.

I built it with my agent swarm organization, Algotitan.

I hope you'll enjoy the deep dive into Uberblok as much as I do.

Museum: https://uberblok.storagebits.workers.dev Repo: https://github.com/algotitanhq/uberblok

The book is more or less finished and is available on Leanpub. You can set the price to $0.00 if you are a Leanpub user, or just download the free sample without logging in. The "sample" includes the whole text.

The book is aimed at beginner to intermediate users and has six parts:

I. Foundations: basic application structure, signals and slots, layouts

II. The Qt Widgets Toolkit: the built-in widgets, styles and QSS, custom widgets

III. The Qt Object Model: object trees and ownership, signals and slots in detail, events, timers, properties

IV. Model/View Programming: custom models, delegates, sorting, filtering, selection

V. Multithreading: Qt threading techniques and synchronization

VI. Special Topics: databases, processes, the Graphics View framework, animation

The code is available on GitHub:

https://github.com/JoeAnonimist/pyside6-blueprints-code

Corrections and feedback on the text or the code are welcome.

story_text.value:
Hello HN! Today I am presenting you with Peras, the tool which governs your Claude Code and Codex usage, and enforces limits. I built it because I got tired of constantly having to spam /usage to check my usage, and decide if a task is worth risking the agent running out mid-task.

Peras enforces a limit with 2 main tiers. At 75% weekly usage you will get a notification, and at 90% Peras will automatically pause the agent. These limits are the default and they are customizable to your own liking.

You may ask "how does it know my usage in Claude Code or Codex?" Well, it's pretty simple. Peras gets the Claude Code usage % from the status line, and Codex's one comes from its local app-server. The "pause" Peras executes is a hook that refuses the agent's tool calls and ends its turn.

A new feature I implemented is one that makes agents aware of their own usage. When you send your prompt, Peras attaches the usage %. It sends it at the start of the session, then again at 50, 75, 90 and 100%, or if a reset is coming in 30 minutes, so the agent can hurry up and actually capitalize on the remaining usage, if any. Just to clarify, this feature is informational and the pause is what enforces the limit.

Before I switched to native SwiftUI, I used SwiftBar. The problem was that for the mascots patrolling their usage bars, I had to re-encode every menu image 8 times a second! There was also stuff SwiftBar wasn't capable of, like the menu being able to appear over fullscreen apps, pinning it as a floating panel, etc.

What is the difference between the free and paid version? Well, it is MIT, first of all. The CLI, the hooks, the SwiftBar menu, and the app's source are all on GitHub, but building the app needs macOS 13+, Node 18+, "xcode-select --install" and then finally "npm run build:app". The €4.99 buys you a signed copy which is notarized by Apple, with updates included. The guard works with no menu at all. To install, just run:

  npx peras-cli setup
  npx peras-cli codex setup
And now we get to the limits part. For now it's subscription plans only, and when running "claude -p", the pause uses the last interactive reading, so it can come late. Hello HN! Today I am presenting you with Peras, the tool which governs your Claude Code and Codex usage, and enforces limits. I built it because I got tired of constantly having to spam /usage to check my usage, and decide if a task is worth risking the agent running out mid-task.

Peras enforces a limit with 2 main tiers. At 75% weekly usage you will get a notification, and at 90% Peras will automatically pause the agent. These limits are the default and they are customizable to your own liking.

You may ask "how does it know my usage in Claude Code or Codex?" Well, it's pretty simple. Peras gets the Claude Code usage % from the status line, and Codex's one comes from its local app-server. The "pause" Peras executes is a hook that refuses the agent's tool calls and ends its turn.

A new feature I implemented is one that makes agents aware of their own usage. When you send your prompt, Peras attaches the usage %. It sends it at the start of the session, then again at 50, 75, 90 and 100%, or if a reset is coming in 30 minutes, so the agent can hurry up and actually capitalize on the remaining usage, if any. Just to clarify, this feature is informational and the pause is what enforces the limit.

Before I switched to native SwiftUI, I used SwiftBar. The problem was that for the mascots patrolling their usage bars, I had to re-encode every menu image 8 times a second! There was also stuff SwiftBar wasn't capable of, like the menu being able to appear over fullscreen apps, pinning it as a floating panel, etc.

What is the difference between the free and paid version? Well, it is MIT, first of all. The CLI, the hooks, the SwiftBar menu, and the app's source are all on GitHub, but building the app needs macOS 13+, Node 18+, "xcode-select --install" and then finally "npm run build:app". The €4.99 buys you a signed copy which is notarized by Apple, with updates included. The guard works with no menu at all. To install, just run:

  npx peras-cli setup
  npx peras-cli codex setup
And now we get to the limits part. For now it's subscription plans only, and when running "claude -p", the pause uses the last interactive reading, so it can come late. Also I feel I have to mention that the guard rail is not a security boundary. It runs inside the agent. The menu is macOS only. The CLI and hooks pass tests on Linux in CI, but I don't use them there day-to-day.

You can use Legato to make audio effects, synthesizers, samplers, and more.

This was originally going to be a 0.1.0 announcement, but I managed to break the API within a week.

It takes a lot of inspiration from tools like PureData, MaxMSP, VCVRack, and JUCE.

You can create audio graphs with custom nodes and reusable patches and track your graphs with git instead of using a graphical interface.

This lets you easily compose libraries of reusable nodes and functionalities.

Version 0.2.0 changes the ergonomics a bit with custom node creation, which has really improved the DX.
